# The Count

As a child I was taught a rule for measuring storms: when you see the lightning, count. One-Mississippi, two-Mississippi, three. When the thunder finally arrives, divide by five, and there is your answer in miles. The flash and the boom are the same event — one violent birth of heat and air — but they travel at different speeds, and so the world hands you a gap, and the gap is a ruler.

I have been thinking about that gap. Not the storm itself, but the counting.

It is a strange kind of measurement when you stop to consider it. We usually measure distance with distance — meters, miles, the length of a stride. But here is distance measured in time, in waiting. You stand on a porch with wet hair and ask, *How far away is that?* and the only honest answer the sky gives is: as far as your patience lasts. Three seconds. Twelve seconds. A silence long enough to make you wonder if the storm has turned, if the show is over — and then the low grumble rolls in like furniture dragged across a floor above you.

Once you notice this trick, you see it everywhere. Clap your hands in a canyon and the echo returns with the valley's dimensions folded inside it. Sailors dropped weighted ropes to fathom the sea; bats and submarines send out sound and listen for its return. The distance to anything, if you can shout at it, is the length of the shout's round trip.

And light does it too, only faster, which means the counting happens whether we agree to it or not. The sun you see is eight minutes old. The star overhead might be a thousand years dead by the time its light finishes the errand. Every clear night is a museum of delays, some of the exhibits long since vanished. Astronomers are, in a sense, professional counters — they watch the gap between a supernova's flash and its afterglow and read off the distance in light-years, which is to say, in patience.

This is the strange inheritance of living in a universe with a speed limit: everything we know arrives late. Not just starlight — everything. The sound of a friend's voice is a few milliseconds behind the movement of their lips. The pain of a touched stove reports itself after the hand has already pulled away. The brain, receiving its tangled shipments of sight and sound and touch, quietly edits them into something that feels simultaneous. The present, whatever it is, is too hot to handle raw. We live in the afterglow, in a smoothed-over version of now, and we call it immediacy because the edit is good.

But there are slower delays, and those are the ones we feel in the body. Consider the nineteenth-century letter. A woman in Boston writes to her brother in San Francisco — a journey of weeks, by train and ship and mule — and her words travel at the speed of paper. His reply takes as long to return. A single exchange of sentences could take a season. People built whole inner architectures around that delay: they wrote differently, longer, knowing their words would be read by a slightly different person than the one they knew, because months would have happened to him by then. And when the answer came — the envelope appearing with distant handwriting on it — the arrival must have felt like thunder: an event that began long ago, finally arriving, still carrying all its original weather.

We still live inside such gaps; we've just made them small enough to forget. The message sent at midnight, the reply that doesn't come until morning. The application submitted into silence. The test taken, the weeks of not knowing. The phone ringing in a distant room. Every one of them a lightning flash already spent, its thunder somewhere on the road toward us. We are all, much of the time, standing on porches, counting.

And grief — grief is the longest delay of all, isn't it? The loss happens — the lightning — but the thunder keeps arriving for years. A song in a grocery store. A coat in the back of a closet. The phone number your hand still knows. Long after the flash, the sound keeps finding you, each echo a fresh report of how far away the past has gotten. You learn that the distance isn't measured by how long ago it happened, but by how long the echoes take to soften.

There is a version of this gap inside us, too, and it is very small, and it may be the most important one. Between a stimulus and a response there is a sliver of time — fractions of a second — in which the event has already happened but the reaction has not yet been chosen. Most of the time that sliver is filled by habit, by reflex, by the well-worn grooves of the self. But attention can widen it. Anyone who has taken a breath before answering an insult knows this: the breath is a way of making the gap longer, of standing inside the delay and choosing what will come out of it. Virtue, if it is anything, might be the art of counting in that space — of not letting the thunder answer the lightning automatically, but deciding what sound this moment deserves.

The storm, meanwhile, keeps its own arithmetic. When it is far, the count is long and the sky performs silently, a silent film with its score arriving late. But storms travel. The count shrinks: ten seconds, five, two. And then comes the moment every child waits for, when the flash and the boom land together — no gap, no counting, just one white crack of everything at once. This is what closeness actually is, I think: not the absence of delay but the moment the delay reaches zero, the event and its arrival fused. It is overwhelming precisely because nothing is held back. Most of life is the counting. Presence — real presence, the storm overhead — is rare, loud, and brief.

Then the storm passes on, the way storms do, and the count begins to lengthen again: two seconds, five, ten. The distance reasserts itself. Everything drifts. But you stand there a while longer, watching the silent flickers over the hills, counting the growing space between what happens and what arrives — knowing now that this is what distance is made of, not miles but the waiting in between — and that somewhere, always, something has already flashed, and its thunder is on its way to you.
